old:
A popular line says loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

A comparison with smoking appears in a 2010 review of 148 studies of about 309,000 people. The review does not itself say loneliness is as harmful as 15 cigarettes a day. A chart in it set the link between social relationships and survival beside smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day, using numbers from different reviews of different people. It was not a head-to-head test.

Most of those studies measured marriage, social networks and support. Loneliness itself was measured in only 8 results.

In about 6,500 people aged 52 and over in England, loneliness was no longer linked with death once age and health at the start were allowed for. Social isolation, meaning little contact with others, still was. Larger recent reviews still link loneliness with a higher risk of dying, less strongly than isolation.

We should act on loneliness because it is painful to live with. That case does not need a comparison with cigarettes.

old:
A popular line says loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

A comparison with smoking appears in a 2010 review that pooled 148 studies of about 309,000 people, followed for 7.5 years on average. The review does not itself say loneliness is as harmful as 15 cigarettes a day. People with stronger social relationships were more likely to be alive at the end. A chart in the paper set that link beside other risk factors, including smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day. The chart used numbers from different reviews of different people. It was not a head-to-head test.

Most of the studies measured marriage, the size of social networks, the support people had and how involved they were with others. Loneliness itself was measured in only 8 results. Within those 8, lonelier people were less likely to survive, but the headline figure is mostly about other things.

Later work gives a more careful picture:

1. A 2015 review of studies that allowed for other factors found loneliness linked with higher odds of dying, about the same as for social isolation and living alone.
2. In about 6,500 people aged 52 and over in England, followed for about 7 years, loneliness was no longer linked with death once age, background and health at the start were allowed for. Social isolation, meaning little contact with others, still was. That does not show that loneliness has no effect on survival: the result was too uncertain to say, and the range that fitted the data included both a lower and a slightly higher risk of dying.
3. Two recent large reviews, one of them of older adults, still find that lonely people have a somewhat higher risk of dying during follow-up. The link is smaller than for isolation and varies a lot between studies.

All of this is observational, so none of it shows cause.

We should take loneliness seriously because it is painful to live with and lowers quality of life. That case does not need a comparison with cigarettes.

Next time you see the slogan, ask which measure it used and whether that measure was loneliness.

old:
In Scottish GP records from 2013 to 2016, people over 90 were among the most likely to miss appointments repeatedly, even after allowing for how many appointments they made. So were people in the most deprived areas. Young adults aged 16 to 30 were also at higher risk, and how a practice ran its appointments contributed too.

In linked Scottish records, people who missed appointments were more likely to die in the following months, especially those with long-term mental health conditions. A missed appointment is a risk marker. The study does not show that missing it causes death, and the figures cover all ages.

A "did not attend" entry records the absence and gives no reason. For an older person, a missed appointment should prompt contact to find out why before any discharge. That is a judgement; no study tested it.

old:
Callers aged 17 to 23 with about two hours of training lowered loneliness scores in a randomised trial in Texas in 2020.

The 240 people taking part were getting Meals on Wheels at home. Each was assigned to one caller, who phoned every weekday in the first week and then as often as the person chose, 2 to 5 times a week, for 4 weeks. Callers were taught to listen and let the person choose the topics. They had no scripts and no therapy training.

On a scale of 3 to 9, loneliness scores fell from 6.5 to 5.2 with calls and from 6.5 to 6.3 without. A second loneliness questionnaire did not show a clear difference. Depression and anxiety scores improved. Physical health scores did not change.

Nobody yet knows whether the benefit lasts once calls stop.

old:
Callers aged 17 to 23 with about two hours of training lowered loneliness scores in a randomised trial in Texas in 2020.

The 240 people taking part were getting Meals on Wheels at home. They were aged 27 to 101 (about 6 in 10 were 65 or over), more than half lived alone, and all had at least one long-term condition. People with cognitive impairment were not included.

The 16 callers were mostly university students. They were taught to listen, to let the person choose what to talk about and to ask about the things the person raised. They had no scripts and no therapy training. Each person was assigned to one caller. Calls came every weekday in the first week, then as often as the person chose, between 2 and 5 a week, for 4 weeks.

On a scale of 3 to 9, loneliness scores fell from 6.5 to 5.2 with calls and from 6.5 to 6.3 without, a difference of about 1 point. There is no agreed size of change that counts as meaningful on these scales. A second loneliness questionnaire did not show a clear difference. Depression and anxiety scores improved. Physical health scores and the size of people's social networks did not change.

Limits: the trial lasted 4 weeks, in the summer of 2020 during the pandemic. More people dropped out of the call group (13) than the comparison group (1). The comparison group got no calls, so the trial gives no answer on whether the listening style or simply being called made the difference. Nobody yet knows whether the benefit lasts once calls stop, and a 2024 review of loneliness programmes for older adults, with searches that ended in June 2021, found too little evidence to judge telephone programmes as a group.

This is one promising result. Befriending services could test the same elements: a regular caller, trained to listen, led by what the person wants to talk about.

More posts in the Care that works series say what made the difference and what was left unmeasured.

old:
Carers were as depressed and anxious after a relative with dementia moved into a care home as they were before the move.

That is from a US study of 1,222 pairs of family carers and relatives with dementia, from 1996 to 2000. In 180 pairs the relative moved into long-term care. Nearly half the carers were then at risk of clinical depression. Husbands and wives were most affected: almost half of spouses visited every day and still helped with their partner's physical care.

We should offer the partner who stays at home their own conversation about how they are managing. That is a judgement. Only a few small trials have looked at support after a move. They did not show clear effects on depression or strain, and the evidence is of very low quality.

You can ask: who will check how I am managing?

That is from a US study of 1,222 pairs of family carers and relatives with dementia, at 6 sites from 1996 to 2000. In 180 pairs the relative moved into long-term care. After the move, nearly half the carers were at risk of clinical depression. Husbands and wives were most affected: almost half of spouses visited every day and still helped with their partner's physical care. Average depression and anxiety scores showed no clear change after the move.

We should offer the partner who stays at home their own conversation about how they are managing. That is a judgement. Only a few small trials have looked at support for carers after a care home move, and they did not show clear effects on depression or strain.

Questions you can ask before and after the move:

1. Who will check how I am managing?
2. How does the fees assessment treat our home and my income if I stay in the house?
3. Can any of the pension stay with me?

This study says nothing about money rules, so ask whoever carries out the fees assessment for the answers. It is also a US study of dementia carers only.

old:
Check on older neighbours who live alone when the weather turns hot.

In the 1995 Chicago heatwave, the people most likely to die were those with medical problems who were confined to bed, and those who did not leave home each day. Living on the top floor and living alone also raised the risk. Friends nearby, working air conditioning and access to transport were linked with lower risk.

In France in 2003, among people aged 65 and over living at home, being unable to get about, poor insulation and sleeping on the top floor right under the roof were linked with dying. Dressing lightly and using ways to cool down were linked with surviving.

Daily checks are a judgement drawn from these studies of who died. The studies show links, not proof of cause.

old:
Check on older neighbours who live alone when the weather turns hot.

In the July 1995 Chicago heatwave, researchers compared 339 people who died with 339 matched neighbours who did not. The people most likely to die were those with medical problems who were confined to bed, and those who did not leave home each day. Living on the top floor and living alone also raised the risk. Having friends nearby or group activities, working air conditioning and access to transport were linked with lower risk.

In the August 2003 heatwave in France, a similar study of people aged 65 and over living at home found that being unable to get about, living in a poorly insulated home and sleeping on the top floor right under the roof were linked with dying. Dressing lightly and using ways to cool down were linked with surviving.

Both studies compared people who died with others who lived, so they show links and not proof of cause. The French study covered people aged 65 and over living at home; the Chicago abstract gives no age limit. They were done in the United States in 1995 and France in 2003.

Our judgement from these studies is that relatives and neighbours should check daily during a heatwave on older people who live alone or rarely go out, especially in top-floor flats, and should help them find ways to cool down. The risk list is also a list of isolation and housing.

Who on your street lives alone and rarely goes out? Say hello before the next hot spell.

old:
All 14 UK studies of welfare rights advice offered in GP surgeries and other health settings reported improved financial security for the people who used it.

That is from a 2022 review of studies from 2010 to 2020. Some also reported better mental health, and some people said their physical health improved. Eight of the 14 studies were case studies, and the review rated their quality as generally poor, so neither the money gain nor the health effects are firmly established. That leaves an evidence gap, and weak studies leave open whether advice improves health.

A second 2022 review of UK free advice services reached a similar view. The studies covered all ages, not only older people.

Health services that see older people on low incomes should offer a route to this advice. That is a judgement. All 14 studies reported a money gain, but their quality was mostly poor, so firm conclusions about money or health are not yet possible.

About 1 in 4 people aged 75 to 85 had been sexually active with a partner in the past year, in a US national survey of 3,005 people aged 57 to 85 (interviewed 2005 to 2006). That was about 4 in 10 men and 1 in 6 women, and women were less likely to have a partner. Among all the sexually active people in the survey (aged 57 to 85), about half had at least one sexual problem that bothered them.

In the same survey, only about 4 in 10 men and 1 in 5 women said they had talked about sex with a doctor since turning 50. The authors noted that both patients and doctors were reluctant to raise it.

English data agree on the main point. In ELSA (6,201 people aged 50 and over, 2012 to 2013), a sizeable minority of men and women were still sexually active in their 70s and 80s. Among those who were sexually active, about 4 in 10 men reported erection problems and about 1 in 3 women reported difficulty with arousal.

Medicines are one reason to ask:

1. Sexual side effects are common with many widely used antidepressants, such as sertraline, citalopram and venlafaxine, and people tend not to mention them unless asked directly. Mirtazapine did not show a clear difference from placebo. These data are not specific to older adults.
2. In a blinded trial of five blood pressure tablets in people aged 45 to 69, men on chlorthalidone had more new erection problems over 2 years than men on placebo, about 17 in 100 compared with 8 in 100. The other four medicines did not differ clearly from placebo, and by 4 years the chlorthalidone difference was no longer clear. A new problem should not automatically be blamed on a blood pressure tablet.

We should ask older patients about sex and intimacy, especially when starting or reviewing medicines. Try: "Has anything changed with sex or intimacy since you started this medicine?"
